title: The War Moves East
subtitle: The Ukrainian counterstrokes, a fighting withdrawal and the violence in Lwów
author: R.G. Cruise
summary: Army Group South advanced through a different battle from the one around Minsk. Soviet counterattacks failed to restore the frontier but complicated German progress, while the capture of Lwów brought a new wave of persecution.
body:
Rain on the roads east

The Southwestern Front’s morning report for 1 July ended with a detail easily lost in accounts of the great tank battles: rain was falling and the unpaved roads were washed out. Above that observation stood the condition of an army group in retreat. The Fifth Army was preparing another attack before withdrawing towards the Sluch. The Sixth, Twenty-sixth and Twelfth Armies were moving through successive positions farther south. Front headquarters had no current information locating the Fourth and Eighth Mechanized Corps. The Fifteenth had been reported around Bilyi Kamin. A war often remembered through spectacular tank numbers was being decided by the ability to move exhausted formations along roads that were becoming harder to use. [1] The retreat followed a series of armoured battles around Lutsk, Dubno and Brody. Soviet counterattacks had not destroyed the German penetration or restored the frontier. They had, however, made Army Group South’s progress different from the devastating encirclement achieved around Minsk. German forces were advancing through western Ukraine, but significant Soviet armies remained capable of withdrawing, defending and attacking again. The distinction mattered to both sides. It bought the Soviet command opportunities while leaving it with severely damaged mechanized formations and the continuing danger of a breakthrough towards the old fortified line. [2] [3] Behind the retreating armies, Lwów had fallen to the Germans on 30 June. Soviet security forces had murdered prisoners before leaving. The new occupiers and local collaborators used the discovery of their bodies to incite violence against Jews. On 1 July the city was experiencing a pogrom, making the change of military control immediately lethal for civilians. [4] The date therefore marks several transitions at once: from counterattack to a fighting withdrawal, from frontier defence towards older fortifications, and from Soviet occupation to German occupation in a city whose inhabitants experienced those regimes in sharply different ways. The purpose of this study is to connect those developments without making one explain away another.

Why the southern advance was different

Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt’s Army Group South had one principal armoured striking force, Ewald von Kleist’s First Panzer Group. Walter von Reichenau’s Sixth Army advanced on the northern part of the Ukrainian sector, while Carl-Heinrich von Stülpnagel’s Seventeenth Army fought farther south towards and beyond Lwów. The German plan sought to destroy Soviet forces west of the Dnieper, using the mobile penetration to cut their retreat. But unlike Army Group Center, Rundstedt did not begin with two panzer groups placed to make a comparable double envelopment around the main opposing deployment. The different arrangement was a constraint on method, not merely a difference in the length of the arrows. [3] Mikhail Kirponos commanded the Soviet Southwestern Front, with Mikhail Potapov’s Fifth Army on its northern wing and Ivan Muzychenko’s Sixth around the Lwów sector. Fyodor Kostenko’s Twenty-sixth and Pavel Ponedelin’s Twelfth extended the front towards the Carpathians and the Romanian approaches. These armies were threatened differently as the German penetration developed. Potapov had to contain the thrust through Volhynia and protect the routes towards Rovno, now Rivne. The armies farther south had to avoid remaining too long in the westward projection around Lwów while German mobile forces moved beyond their northern flank. [5] [6] The operational geography was more intricate than an open Ukrainian plain. The Western Bug marked the initial crossing; the Styr, Ikva and Horyn divided subsequent routes. Around Brody and Berestechko, smaller rivers ran through marshy valleys with limited bridges and causeways. The Fifteenth Mechanized Corps’ after-action report listed five significant water obstacles in its intended attack zone and described swampy approaches, restricted roads and commanding ground held by the enemy. Tanks were numerous, but places where they could cross and deploy were not. [7] The German advance consequently faced both Soviet resistance and the practical need to protect its own communications. A formation pushing east beyond Dubno could become vulnerable to attacks from the south or north against the road behind it. Diverting troops to defeat those attacks reduced the force immediately available to move farther east. This was the operational value of the Soviet counterstrokes even when their original objectives were not achieved. It did not make every attack well directed, nor did it make the losses sustainable. It meant that German progress depended on defeating active opponents rather than simply exploiting an empty rear. [3]

The corps that had tanks but lacked a complete force

The counterattack programme described in the study for 25 June required attacks from opposite sides of the German penetration. The Eighth and Fifteenth Mechanized Corps were central to the southern blow; the Ninth and Nineteenth were assigned to Potapov’s northern grouping. The Fourth Corps also supplied forces and fought in the Lwów sector. These were substantial formations on organizational charts, but their inventories cannot be added together and treated as the strength of one simultaneous battle. Units arrived at different times, received changing tasks and sometimes operated apart from their parent corps. [8] The Fifteenth Corps offers a particularly revealing case because its commander’s subsequent report explains what was missing. The corps entered the war under Ignaty Karpezo. Its Thirty-seventh Tank Division had an incomplete motorized infantry regiment far from the division and without transport. Some artillery lacked the tractors necessary to move it. The 212th Motorized Division had men but almost no vehicles for carrying them, their weapons or their supplies. Corps signals and engineer units were still being formed and trained. A formation could therefore contain modern tanks while lacking the infantry, bridging and communications needed to make those tanks effective. [7] Those deficiencies became visible in the movements of the first week. The report describes a tank regiment delayed in marshy ground, artillery still coming from training areas, and divisions turned from one assembly area towards another. It also records that the order prescribing the morning attack on 25 June reached the corps at 8.30 that morning—after the seven o’clock start specified by front headquarters. This is a more precise explanation of missed timing than a general assertion that Soviet officers were slow or incompetent. The attack schedule had already expired before this headquarters received it. [7] [9] Command itself was disrupted by attack. The corps report dates the bombing that incapacitated Karpezo to the evening of 26 June and states that his deputy, Colonel Yermolayev, took over. That dated record is preferable to carrying Karpezo’s name across the entire battle or assuming that a change of commander occurred on the invasion’s first day. German air action mattered here not only because it might destroy tanks. It could wound the people organizing a corps, displace its headquarters and consume time needed to coordinate an attack. [7]

What a unit name conceals

“Motorized” was sometimes an aspiration

The Fifteenth Corps report described the 212th Motorized Division as lacking vehicles even for essential movement and supply. Its name identified its intended organization; it did not prove that its infantry could keep pace with tanks. Reading a corps as a complete combined-arms force simply because its component units existed on paper exaggerates the strength available in battle. [7]

The counterstroke reaches the German communications

The attack towards Dubno was not wholly imaginary. The Southwestern Front’s report for the night of 27 June states that the Eighth Mechanized Corps had begun its counteroffensive from the Radziwiłłów area at nine that morning, with Dubno as its objective by the end of the day. Its leading detachment had passed Sytne at 11.30 without contact with the enemy. The same report located the Fifteenth Corps around Toporiv, reorganizing for its own attack towards Berestechko. The two entries show movement and preparation existing side by side, rather than a single coordinated mass advancing in line. [10] A group from Dmitry Ryabyshev’s Eighth Corps, associated with brigade commissar Nikolai Popel and elements of the Twelfth and Thirty-fourth Tank Divisions, penetrated towards Dubno and threatened important German communications. Aleksey Isaev’s reconstruction distinguishes this real disruption from Popel’s later, more dramatic account of entering Dubno and capturing senior German officers. German forces redirected against the penetration, including Hans-Valentin Hube’s Sixteenth Panzer Division, cut the Soviet group off. The result was a dangerous interruption of the German advance followed by the isolation of the troops that had produced it. A claim that Dubno was securely retaken would overstate the result; a claim that the counterstroke achieved nothing would miss its effect on German movements. [11] The Fifteenth Corps’ parallel effort shows why the wider counteroffensive did not develop around that penetration. Its report describes an intended advance of forty kilometres towards Berestechko, across a zone with several difficult water obstacles. The staff considered the available strength inadequate for the assigned task and judged that a narrower attack against German communications was more realistic. Orders to withdraw and then resume the offensive further disrupted the corps’ preparations. These retrospective explanations are partly a commander’s account of failure and must be read as such. They are nonetheless unusually specific about the relation between the task, time and available means. [7] On 28 June, the Tenth Tank Division could not force the Ostrivka crossing over a causeway under German artillery and antitank fire. Yermolayev sent a liaison officer to obtain support from the attached Eighth Tank Division. The officer’s car was hit and burned; the wounded messenger reached the division through fields and gullies. Two tanks sent on the same mission were also set on fire. The account makes the command problem tangible. Cooperation depended on a messenger physically crossing ground the enemy could already fire across. [7] The Thirty-seventh Tank Division also struggled at the crossings near Stanyslavchyk. Tanks attempting to bypass a bridge became stuck in marshy ground and were hit by artillery. The corps eventually withdrew from the exposed area between the rivers rather than sacrifice the remaining force there. This was a defeat imposed by terrain, German fire and inadequate coordination together. It was not simply a contest in which one tank model proved superior to another, and it cannot be explained by Luftwaffe bombing alone. [7]

A timetable for retreat, not a recovered front

At eleven on the night of 30 June, Kirponos issued a new programme. The Southwestern Front was to withdraw towards the Korosten, Novograd-Volynskiy, Shepetovka, Starokonstantinov and Proskurov fortified regions by 9 July, while holding an intermediate line until 6 July. The order acknowledged German control of the Dubno–Ostrog–Rovno area after stubborn fighting. It also recognized danger from the north, where German forces had reached Bobruisk, and from concentrations in northeastern Romania. The southern armies were no longer dealing only with the battle immediately in front of them. Their flanks belonged to a widening campaign. [5] The withdrawal was assigned stages rather than a single destination. Potapov’s Fifth Army was to begin moving after darkness on 1 July, reach intermediate positions on the Styr and Horyn, and arrive at the Sluch by the morning of the 5th. The Sixth Army received its own sequence through Ostrog, Kremenets and Volochisk. The Twenty-sixth and Twelfth Armies had routes farther south. Mechanized corps were to regroup behind them, and aviation was ordered to protect their movement while continuing to strike the German penetration. These dates establish what the command wanted to achieve. They do not demonstrate that all the intermediate positions were reached or held as prescribed. [5] The morning summary on 1 July shows the first reality against which that programme had to operate. The Fifth Army was still combining an attack south towards Mizoch with preparations to withdraw. A German attempt to cross the Horyn the previous afternoon was reported repulsed. The Sixth Army was moving through positions east of Lwów, while the Twenty-sixth withdrew from the approaches south of the city. The front could still describe an army-level operation, but it admitted that the whereabouts of two mechanized corps were unknown. This was more coherent than the Western Front’s condition around Minsk, yet far from an orderly march by intact formations. [1] The old fortified regions offered positions around which defence might be rebuilt. They were not a continuous wall capable of compensating automatically for missing troops, ammunition or communications. Kirponos’s order explicitly required field forces, especially artillery and antitank weapons, to organize the defence around them. That requirement explains why the withdrawal schedule mattered. Fortifications could become useful only if enough men and equipment reached them before German mobile forces broke through or passed around them. [5] The same order assigned the Forty-ninth Rifle Corps a task distinct from the retreat of the forward armies. Its 190th and 197th Rifle Divisions were to march from Volochisk on the morning of 1 July and occupy fortifications around Liakhovtsy, Bazaliya and Sharlaevka that evening. Kirponos was trying to put troops into the receiving position while the battered mobile formations moved behind it. The corps offered the possibility of a defended destination rather than merely another line towards which exhausted units could be told to withdraw. Whether that possibility became effective depended on arrivals and coordination: the order also allotted separate routes and successive assembly areas to the Fourth, Eighth and Fifteenth Mechanized Corps. Preserving those formations required space on the roads as well as permission to retreat. [5]

A deadline that can be checked

9 July belonged to a Soviet plan

The 30 June order set 9 July for the front’s withdrawal to the fortified regions and 6 July for holding the intermediate line. These are documented benchmarks. They should be compared with later positions rather than converted into a claim that the whole front was safely established on schedule. [5]

For German headquarters, the southern fighting was already a warning against assuming uniform results across the front. Blau’s official study describes repeated Soviet counterattacks and an advance below German expectations. That is a contemporary expectation reconstructed from the German records, not a licence to invent a deadline for Kiev. By 1 July, the Germans had gained substantial ground and defeated the immediate Soviet counteroffensive; they had not destroyed the Southwestern Front in a counterpart to the Minsk encirclement. Both parts of that judgment are necessary. [3]

Lwów’s prisons and the change of occupier

The German capture of Lwów, today Lviv, exposed the bodies of prisoners killed by Soviet security personnel during the retreat. The city’s Łąckiego prison was one site of the murders. Research presented by Lviv’s Center for Urban History dates the killings there to the night of 23–24 June and relates them to the Soviet decision to eliminate political detainees rather than permit their release as the Germans approached. The victims of Soviet repression came from several communities. Their murder was a crime committed by the Soviet authorities, and the hurried military withdrawal does not alter that responsibility. [12] The discovery also created an opportunity for German propaganda. Bodies were displayed, relatives searched for missing people, and Jews were forced into the work of removing and arranging the dead. The occupiers and nationalist activists falsely assigned collective responsibility for Soviet crimes to the city’s Jews. Jews had themselves been among the victims of Soviet repression. The political use of the corpses therefore required a deliberate substitution: the actual institutions responsible for the prison murders were replaced by an ethnic and religious population available for persecution. [12] This is a point at which historical precision has moral consequences. Acknowledging the NKVD killings does not validate the accusation against Jews; identifying the false accusation does not diminish the prisoners’ deaths. The crimes had different perpetrators and victims. They were connected through the use the new occupiers made of the first crime to encourage another. Treating the sequence as an undifferentiated exchange of communal revenge would reproduce the perpetrators’ explanation instead of examining it. The political transition in the city was also contested within the invading coalition. On 30 June, Yaroslav Stetsko proclaimed a Ukrainian state in the name of Stepan Bandera’s wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, the OUN-B. The declaration sought to use the German advance to establish national authority. German leaders had their own plans for exploiting and governing Ukraine, and would reject the proclamation and arrest its leaders. Those later measures do not mean that OUN-B activists had been uninvolved in cooperation with the Germans or anti-Jewish persecution at the moment of conquest. [13] The NARA study also reproduces evidence of the organization’s antisemitic programme. This matters because the persecution was not simply an unplanned emotional response to bodies found in a prison. Existing political ideas, the ambitions of nationalist activists and German occupation policy helped shape the violence. The new state proclaimed by Stetsko was neither a democratic settlement accepted by the city’s different communities nor a government Germany had agreed to recognize. Its immediate history must be understood within those limits. [13]

The pogrom on 1 July

John-Paul Himka’s study of the Lviv pogrom distinguishes the roles of German forces, the Ukrainian nationalist militia and the participating urban crowd. German occupation created the setting and encouraged violence; militia members seized Jews and brought them into the sites of abuse; civilians joined in robbery, humiliation and assault. The crowd included both Poles and Ukrainians. Naming these participants is more accurate than assigning guilt to an entire national population, and it prevents the category “local violence” from obscuring the role of the occupiers. [14] The violence targeted women as well as men and included sexual assault and public degradation. Jews forced to handle the prison dead were attacked under an accusation they could not answer by proving their innocence, because the accusation concerned their identity rather than any individual act. German forces also carried out shootings. Himka’s analysis therefore resists a clean division between a civilian mob and an entirely separate official killing operation: their actions interacted, although particular acts still require specific attribution. [14] The pogrom’s death toll is less certain than its occurrence and perpetrators. The Holocaust Memorial Museum gives at least several hundred victims, possibly more, and warns that familiar totals combine the pogrom with German executions over a longer part of July. Four thousand should therefore not be presented as an agreed count for 1 July alone. Separating those events preserves their chronology without diminishing the crime. [4]

Counting different events

Why familiar totals can mislead

Some estimates combine the early pogrom, prison shootings and later executions. A total for that wider sequence cannot be assigned automatically to the mob violence of 1 July. The event is securely documented even where its exact death toll remains uncertain. [4]

The operational record and the social record now describe the same city from different directions. Soviet armies were moving east through successive lines; the people left behind were encountering a new distribution of power over their bodies, homes and lives. The end of one occupation did not produce a general condition of liberation. Relief at the departure of Soviet institutions could coexist with, or be mobilized into, participation in German persecution. The historical task is to identify those choices and institutions without allowing a later national narrative to decide in advance whose suffering or culpability belongs in the account. [13]

Riga and the unequal movement of the war

Far to the north, German troops occupied Riga on 1 July as Army Group North expanded its position on the Western Dvina. The evening German map shows an advance distributed across several crossings and routes, not one uniform line sweeping through Latvia. The Soviet Northwestern Front’s intelligence report that evening described German concentrations near the river, reconnaissance between Pļaviņas and Krāslava, and movement from the Jēkabpils–Līvāni sector towards Madona and Gulbene. It also recorded air reconnaissance around Tallinn and Pskov. The pressure was spreading beyond the initial river crossings towards the next defensive area. [15] [16] That northern progress should sharpen the comparison with Ukraine rather than draw this study away from it. In the Baltic region, German mobile forces had reached and crossed the Dvina while Soviet armies struggled to reassemble. In the centre, the Minsk pockets were still being reduced as the advance approached another river barrier. In the south, Soviet counterattacks had imposed a more sustained interruption, and the armies around Lwów were withdrawing instead of being trapped together in a great enclosure. The three sectors were parts of one invasion, but they were not keeping the same operational time. [2] The most useful measure of the Ukrainian counterattacks is consequently neither the highest tank total quoted for the battle nor a declaration that they “saved” the Soviet Union. They failed in their immediate purpose of defeating the German mobile grouping. They also forced the Germans to fight for communications and crossings, contributed to a slower southern advance and left substantial Soviet armies still in the field. Their cost weakened the mobile forces those armies would need in the next stage. Success and failure operated at different levels, and a responsible account must retain both. [5] [7] [3] By 1 July, the war was moving east, but it was carrying unresolved military and human consequences with it. The German armies had won ground and imposed severe losses. Soviet headquarters were trying to convert surviving forces, reserves and older fortifications into a new defence. Civilians behind the advance were already experiencing the violence built into German conquest, intensified through local participation and the manipulation of Soviet crimes. Two days later Stalin would address the population directly. His speech and the measures surrounding it would expose the scale of the emergency, and the difference between announcing a national war effort and making it work.

sourceMethod: Numbered notes link to the source list and return to their first use. Page and document references accompany the relevant notes. German situation maps and staff reports are evidence of what German headquarters recorded, not an omniscient picture of the battlefield. Soviet operational records are cited from the General Staff’s published documentary collections, accessed in transcription; archival identifiers are those printed in those collections. Orders establish intentions; they do not by themselves prove execution. Postwar military accounts are checked against dated records and identified as retrospective. Place names follow familiar historical usage, with present-day equivalents where useful.
